title: Redwood Optimize walkthrough - batching + KV cache cost model (Verdant Payments)
summary: Walkthrough of Redwood Optimize recommendations focused on batching and prefix/KV cache strategies with an attached cost model. Covered typical hit-rate expectations, latency impact, tradeoffs between hosted vs dedicated, network/VPC considerations, and a proposed pilot (2-week benchmark run). Customer concerned about P99 latency, data residency, and KMS integration.
topics: Batching: dynamic vs fixed, target batch sizes, latency tail behavior
Prefix caching: script-level caching and dedup for repetitive prompts
KV cache: hit-rate assumptions, memory sizing, eviction policies
Cost model: per-token cost assumptions, CPU vs GPU, autoscaling bursts
Deployment: hosted vs dedicated, VPC/KMS/SOC2 questions
Next steps: benchmark pilot, share spreadsheet, security docs
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Alex from Redwood, with Priya and Jordan. We'll run through Optimize — batching, prefix and KV cache, and the cost model.
[00:12] John Liu: Great. We are mostly interested in reducing token costs for chat and also keeping P99 under 450ms for the main flows.
[00:21] Priya Nair: Perfect. Quick qual — what's your current setup? Marcus, you mentioned you have a mix of in-house embeddings and a 3rd-party chat api?
[00:30] Marcus Reid: Yeah, right now we ship to a hosted LLM endpoint, using about 200 req/s peak, average 80, about 10-20 tokens per turn. We're seeing high tails at peak especially when session context grows.
[00:45] Sara Gomez: Also most requests are templated customer support prompts, so there's a lot of repetitive prefixes.
[00:52] Alex Carter: Good. That pattern maps really well to prefix caching and KV cache. We'll demo the numbers.
[00:58] [00:58] Priya Nair: Slide 3 — high-level: batching reduces GPU overhead by amortizing kernel launch and attention compute across requests. For throughput-limited workloads batching lowers unit cost, but it can impact latency—tradeoff depends on SLO.
[01:15] John Liu: Can you quantify? We need to know if batching will blow our P99.
[01:19] Priya Nair: Totally — for a small model (7B), we've seen 2x-3x cost reduction at 100ms median if you allow 40-60ms extra latency. For larger models (30B+) improvements are larger because kernel overhead is higher. But the real lever is adaptive batching.
[01:35] Marcus Reid: Adaptive?
[01:36] Priya Nair: We mean continuous batching in the runtime: requests are batched opportunistically with a tight micro-slo for latency. If the queue doesn't fill within X ms, the batch is flushed. So you get most of the cost benefits at low latency hit.
[01:49] Alex Carter: Example numbers — with an expected arrival rate of 200 rps and average seq length 60 tokens, dynamic batching gave Verdana — sorry, Verdant — about 1.8x lower per-token cost in our pilot. (laughter)
[02:06] Sara Gomez: Haha, thanks.
[02:09] Priya Nair: Prefix caching: because your prompts are templated, the first N tokens (the prefix) can be cached in the KV cache. If you cache the KV for commonly used prefixes, subsequent completions only compute from the tail which reduces tokens and GPU work.
[02:23] [02:23] John Liu: What hit-rate should we plan for? Our templating is about 60% shared intro, 30% semi variable, 10% custom free-form.
[02:35] Priya Nair: With that distribution we typically model a 45-65% cache hit rate on prefix cache if you include some canonicalization. If you precompute prefix hashes in your client and route through Redwood's cache keys, it's higher.
[02:48] Marcus Reid: How do you canonicalize? We're worried about small diffs like customer name or ticket id causing misses.
[02:55] Priya Nair: We recommend placeholder tokens for entity substitution, and then post-process formatting. So the cache key uses the templated structure rather than full text. Also safe to set a short TTL for ephemeral fields.
[03:09] [03:09] Alex Carter: KV cache sizing: For a model with 30k context and avg prefix KV size ~1.2MB per prefix, if you want to support 10k hot prefixes you'd need ~12GB of memory, plus overhead. We include eviction policies LRU with warm-up preloading for known templates.
[03:28] John Liu: 12GB sounds heavy. Can you do compression or quantized KV?
[03:33] Priya Nair: Yes — we do compressed KV in memory and can quantize the stored cache. That typically reduces mem by ~30-40% at some CPU decompression overhead. There's also a probabilistic bloom-filter layer to avoid unnecessary load.
[03:47] Sara Gomez: Ok, walk us through the cost model — how do you calculate per-token savings?
[03:52] Alex Carter: We sent a spreadsheet but here's the quick math: baseline hosted per-token cost = model compute cost + infra amortized + overhead. With batching you see compute cost per token drop because of higher GPU utilization. With prefix/KV cache you reduce tokens generated and context compute — effectively saving both compute and memory bandwidth.
[04:12] [04:12] Priya Nair: In the example we ran for a mid-sized payments customer: baseline $0.008 per 1k tokens. With adaptive batching + 50% prefix hit we got to $0.0035 per 1k tokens — so ~55% savings. Numbers vary by seq length.
[04:29] Marcus Reid: Those per-1k numbers are great but what's the P99 impact at peak?
[04:33] Priya Nair: We measured P99 increased by ~20-60ms in most cases with a flush timeout of 30ms. For mission-critical flows we recommend 15ms flush timeout with smaller batch multipliers—still nets 20-30% savings without compromising tail.
[04:49] John Liu: What about dedicated capacity vs hosted? We're considering dedicated for compliance.
[04:54] Alex Carter: Dedicated gives you guaranteed GPU pools and more predictable latency, and data isolation. Cost is higher upfront (reserved commits) but you control autoscale policies and can tune batch sizes tightly. Hosted is more cost-efficient for spiky/variable workloads and faster to deploy. For Verdant Payments, if you need VPC/KMS and SOC2, Redwood Private in a VPC with customer-managed KMS is common.
[05:17] Aisha Khan (Security): On KMS — we need to ensure keys never leave our control. Do you integrate with AWS KMS/HSM?
[05:24] Jordan Lee: Yes we support bring-your-own KMS and HSM options for Private deployments; we can also provide audit logs for key usage. We'll share the security whitepaper.
[05:33] [05:33] Sara Gomez: Any gotchas for session KV across restarts? If an instance dies, do we lose cache warm-up?
[05:39] Priya Nair: For Dedicated we have sharded persistent KV backed by SSD with fast warm-up. For hosted we keep a distributed cache layer with replication; warm-up hits the bloom filter and we can pre-warm common prefixes. There's a short cold-start penalty but it's bounded.
[05:54] John Liu: Can we run a pilot to validate both hit-rate and P99 under our traffic shape?
[05:59] Alex Carter: Absolutely. Typical pilot — 2 weeks: first week we run in shadow mode (no user-facing routing) to collect prefix distributions and hit-rate estimates, then a 1-week controlled canary with 10-20% traffic. We'll run bench marks and share raw telemetry.
[06:14] [06:14] Marcus Reid: What's the instrumentation we need to add client-side?
[06:18] Priya Nair: A small SDK call to compute prefix hash and a header to indicate freshness; we can accept precomputed keys too. Also we'll want request-level metadata: template id, session length, latency SLO tags.
[06:30] John Liu: Security signoff timeline — SOC2 and legal review may take 6-8 weeks.
[06:36] Aisha Khan: We'll need the SOC2 artefacts and an MDR for incident response.
[06:41] Alex Carter: We'll send SOC2 report, redacted pen-test summary, and the KMS integration guide.
[06:47] [06:47] Priya Nair: Back to cost model detail — the spreadsheet (link shared) assumes: 1) baseline request size, 2) arrival distribution, 3) cache hit rate scenarios 20/40/60/80%, 4) batching flush thresholds 15/30/50ms. We modeled both per-token compute and amortized infra.
[07:05] Sara Gomez: Could you run numbers for our nightly reconciliation job? That's high token counts but latency tolerant.
[07:12] Priya Nair: Yes — those are ideal for very large batch sizes or reserved dedicated runs; you can push throughput and drop unit costs significantly.
[07:20] John Liu: Competitors? Are there other ways to do this in-house or with providers?
[07:24] Alex Carter: You can build custom batching + cache, but it's operationally heavy. Competitors like Anthropic or OpenAI have hosted endpoints without the same KV cache primitives; some infra providers like Vertex have autoscaling but less inference-optimized runtimes. We'll include a competitor comparison note.
[07:42] [07:42] Marcus Reid: Any SLO templates we can look at?
[07:45] Priya Nair: Yes we'll share our recommended SLOs: median latency target, P95/P99 thresholds, and fallback policies (model-variant fallback and region fallback).
[07:56] John Liu: One more — how do you handle billing attribution when using cache? If two customers hit the same prefix, is that a meter confusion?
[08:04] Jordan Lee: Cache keys are namespaced per-customer in Private and Dedicated; in hosted the cache is per-tenant. Billing attribution is always per-customer.
[08:13] [08:13] Alex Carter: Ok, quick recap and next steps. We'll: 1) share updated cost model spreadsheet with Verdant numbers, 2) send SOC2 + KMS docs, 3) schedule pilot kickoff for 2/7, 4) run shadow week then 1-week canary.
[08:29] Sara Gomez: Sounds good.
[08:31] John Liu: Can you include a recommended flush timeout and batch multiplier for our traffic?
[08:36] Priya Nair: We'll recommend 15ms flush timeout for user-facing SLO and a batch multiplier tuned to expected rps. We'll include two scenarios in the spreadsheet.
[08:46] [08:46] Alex Carter: Great — thanks everyone.
[08:49] [08:49] End of recording.

Notes: transcription contains minor mis-hearings (e.g., Verdana -> Verdant). Shared artifacts: https://redwood.example.com/spreadsheets/verdant-cost-model (shared), Security whitepaper link: https://redwood.example.com/security/whitepaper.pdf
